Higher-order Gaussian bounds for maximally subelliptic boundary value problems

Brian Street Note: The author was partially supported by National Science Foundation Grant 2153069.
Abstract

We establish higher-order Gaussian upper bounds for the heat semigroups associated with a broad class of sectorial maximally subelliptic quadratic forms on manifolds with boundary. Near non-characteristic boundary points and in the interior, we obtain pointwise bounds for all mixed derivatives of the heat kernel in time and along the Hörmander vector fields, expressed in the associated Carnot–Carathéodory geometry. The results apply to operators of arbitrary even order, systems, nonsymmetric forms, and boundary conditions beyond the Dirichlet case.

1 Introduction

In this paper, we establish higher-order Gaussian bounds near the non-characteristic boundary (see Definition 1.10) and in the interior for heat semigroups whose generators correspond to certain maximally subelliptic quadratic forms. These are quadratic forms defined in terms of Hörmander vector fields which satisfy a maximally subelliptic estimate (see Assumption 1.1), and they can be viewed as maximally subelliptic boundary value problems; we do not restrict attention to Dirichlet boundary conditions. To establish these bounds, we use the abstract result proved in [Str25c], which was developed with this paper in mind. This is the fourth paper in a series studying general maximally subelliptic boundary value problems. The first [Str25a] and third [Str26] papers in the series play key roles in the proof.

The main technical theorem of this paper is Theorem 3.14; however, Corollary 4.7 is easier to use in practice. In this introduction, we state a further corollary (Corollary 1.4), which is easier to understand and already covers some of the main examples.

On manifolds without boundary, the interior theory of Gaussian estimates for subelliptic heat kernels is by now well developed. For second-order Hörmander operators, estimates for the heat kernel and its time and vector-field derivatives are known in a variety of settings; see, for example, [SC84, JSC86, KS87, KS88, BLU02, BBLU10, BB23]. Higher-order analogues have also been obtained on homogeneous, nilpotent, and polynomial-growth Lie groups; see [Heb89, tER98, tERS97, Dun01, Dun05]. Beyond nilpotent Lie groups, the author established interior higher-order Gaussian bounds for heat operators corresponding to non-negative symmetric maximally subelliptic operators in [Str23, Theorem 8.4.2]; this result was then generalized to possibly nonsymmetric operators in [Str25c, Theorem ] (see [Str25c, Section ] for examples). In particular, some of these results allow complex coefficients and give estimates for derivatives of arbitrary order. These interior results do not, however, address the boundary phenomena considered here.

The corresponding boundary theory is less developed. Much of the existing literature on subelliptic heat operators on domains concerns the Dirichlet heat kernel or the initial-Dirichlet problem; see, for example, [LSC14, CC21, GM18]. Some such Dirichlet results also allow nonsymmetric forms. There are results for particular non-Dirichlet problems, such as the ∂¯\bar{\partial}-Neumann problem [PS12], but these concern boundary conditions tied to a specific operator or geometric structure. In contrast, we begin with a sectorial quadratic form and its domain, which together determine the boundary conditions. The Dirichlet problem is included, but we do not restrict attention to it: the framework also permits free or natural boundary conditions and, in higher order, problems in which only a selected subset of the traces

Xj​f|∂𝔑,0≤j≤κ−1,\left.X^{j}f\right|_{\partial\mathfrak{N}},\qquad 0\leq j\leq\kappa-1,

is prescribed, with the remaining boundary conditions induced by the form; see Example 1.8. To our knowledge, no existing general result simultaneously treats arbitrary order 2​κ2\kappa, systems, nonsymmetric sectorial forms, form-induced boundary conditions not restricted to the Dirichlet case, and bounds for arbitrary time and derivatives along the Hörmander vector fields up to non-characteristic boundary points.

In the elliptic setting, heat-kernel estimates on domains are available for substantially broader classes of boundary conditions, including Robin and other form-defined conditions; see, for example, [AtE97, Dan00, AW03, Ouh04, Cla12, BCE25]. These works use different methods and address different difficulties.

Remark 1.9.

The reader unfamiliar with the general theory of maximal subellipticity and the difficulties that can arise can find an introduction in [Str23, Chapter 1].

AI Usage.

Once a nearly final draft of this paper was written, and after the mathematical content and proofs were complete, the author used ChatGPT for proofreading and improving the exposition. Otherwise, this article is human generated.

1.1 Non-characteristic points

Definition 1.10.

We say that ξ∈∂𝔑\xi\in\partial\mathfrak{N} is WW-non-characteristic if there exists jj such that Wj​(ξ)∉Tξ​∂𝔑W_{j}(\xi)\notin T_{\xi}\partial\mathfrak{N}. Equivalently, ∂𝔑\partial\mathfrak{N} is non-characteristic near ξ\xi, in the classical sense, for the operator f↦(W1​f,…,Wr​f)f\mapsto\left(W_{1}f,\ldots,W_{r}f\right).

Kohn and Nirenberg [KN65], Derridj [Der72], and Jerison [Jer81a, Jer81b] first pointed out that whether a boundary point is WW-non-characteristic has important implications for the subellipticity of operators such as ℒ\mathscr{L}. Indeed, Jerison [Jer81b] showed that, even for the sub-Laplacian on the Heisenberg group in a simple model domain, hypoellipticity for the Dirichlet problem can fail at a characteristic boundary point. This observation helps explain why we restrict attention to non-characteristic boundary points.

In the above setting, ∂Ω\partial\Omega consists entirely of WW-non-characteristic points. In fact, given any ξ0∈∂𝔑\xi_{0}\in\partial\mathfrak{N}, one can pick XX as above such that ξ0∈Ω\xi_{0}\in\Omega if and only if ξ0\xi_{0} is WW-non-characteristic.

Many of the results on which this work is based apply only near WW-non-characteristic points; examples include the main results of [Str25a] (see Theorem 2.4) and [Str26]. Furthermore, although they do not play a direct role in this work, the trace theorems established in [Str25b] work well near WW-non-characteristic boundary points (see [Str25b, Chapter ]) but less well near WW-characteristic boundary points (see [Str25b, Section ]). This will be used in forthcoming work on maximally subelliptic boundary value problems, based on this paper.

1.2 Outline of the proof

Both the statement and the proof of our main technical theorem (Theorem 3.14) are somewhat technical. However, the basic outline of the proof is easier to understand. The main ideas are as follows.

  1. 1.

    [Str26] shows that ∂t+ℒ\partial_{t}+\mathscr{L} and ∂t+ℒ∗\partial_{t}+\mathscr{L}^{*} are subelliptic on (0,∞)×Ω(0,\infty)\times\Omega, and therefore hypoelliptic. As a consequence, the function Kt​(ξ,η)K_{t}(\xi,\eta) in Corollary 1.4 is smooth on (0,∞)×Ω×Ω(0,\infty)\times\Omega\times\Omega; see Proposition 5.6. The subelliptic estimates have their roots in work of Kohn and Nirenberg [KN65] and Kohn [Koh78].

  2. 2.

    [Str25a] provides scaling maps adapted to the Carnot–Carathéodory geometry given by ρW\rho_{W}; see Section 2. Using these scaling maps, for δ\delta small, one can rescale BW​(ξ,δ)B_{W}(\xi,\delta) to be essentially the unit ball, in such a way that δ2​κ​ℒ\delta^{2\kappa}\mathscr{L} is rescaled to a new operator on the unit ball ℒξ,δ\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta} where ℒξ,δ\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta} satisfies maximally subelliptic estimates similar to those satisfied by ℒ\mathscr{L}, uniformly in ξ\xi and δ\delta. The scaling has its roots in ideas of Nagel, Stein, and Wainger [NSW85] and Tao and Wright [TW03], and is based on results of Stovall and the author [SS18].

  3. 3.

    The subelliptic estimates from [Str26] apply uniformly to ∂t+ℒξ,δ\partial_{t}+\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta}. These imply hypoelliptic estimates for ∂t+ℒξ,δ\partial_{t}+\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta}, which are uniform in ξ\xi and δ\delta. See, for example, Lemmas 5.26 and 5.27.

  4. 4.

    Undoing the scaling from 2, the hypoelliptic estimates from 3 turn into hypoelliptic estimates for ∂t+δ2​κℒ\partial_{t}+\delta^{2\kappa}\mathscr{L} on BV​(ξ,δ)B_{V}(\xi,\delta), which are appropriately uniform in ξ\xi and δ\delta. Similarly, one also obtains hypoelliptic estimates for ∂t+δ2​κℒ∗\partial_{t}+\delta^{2\kappa}\mathscr{L}^{*} which are appropriately uniform in ξ\xi and δ\delta. See Proposition 5.16.

  5. 5.

    Such hypoelliptic estimates, uniform across base points and scales, constitute the main hypothesis of [Str25c, Theorem ], which in turn gives the desired higher-order Gaussian bounds (1.5). The proof of [Str25c, Theorem ] is based on ideas of Jerison and Sánchez-Calle [JSC86] and Hebisch [Heb89].

A principal source of technicality in this paper is the uniformity required in 4, and hence in 2 and 3. We must therefore keep track of what the various constants in our inequalities depend on and of the order of the quantifiers. Thus, the statements of many of our estimates contain a series of quantifiers whose ordering is an essential part of the estimate.

1.3 A motivation

Although the results of this paper are of independent interest, a principal motivation for this paper is to facilitate the study of parametrices for homogeneous maximally subelliptic boundary value problems. Indeed, if (ℒ,Dom⁡(ℒ))(\mathscr{L},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})) is as in Section 1, then

S:=∫01T⁡(t)​𝑑tS:=\int_{0}^{1}T(t)\>dt

is a parametrix for ℒ\mathscr{L} on Ω\Omega. Indeed, [EN06, Chapter 2, Lemma 1.3] shows

ℒ​S​f=f−T⁡(1)​f,∀f∈L2​(𝔑,Vol),\mathscr{L}Sf=f-T(1)f,\quad\forall f\in L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol}),
S​ℒ​f=f−T⁡(1)​f,∀f∈Dom⁡(ℒ)⊇𝒟0​(𝔑).S\mathscr{L}f=f-T(1)f,\quad\forall f\in\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})\supseteq\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N}).

Since T⁡(1)T(1) is given by integration against a smooth function on Ω×Ω\Omega\times\Omega (by Corollary 1.4), this shows that SS is a two-sided parametrix for ℒ\mathscr{L} on Ω\Omega. The estimates for Kt​(ξ,η)K_{t}(\xi,\eta) in Corollary 1.4 can then be used to prove good mapping properties for this parametrix. For a discussion of these ideas on manifolds without boundary, see [Str25c, Section ]. In a future paper, we will use these ideas to deduce sharp regularity properties for maximally subelliptic boundary value problems.

2 Scaling

Before we can state our main theorem (Theorem 3.14), we need to introduce the main theorem of [Str25a], though we state it slightly differently than that reference. This result gives scaling maps which turn small Carnot–Carathéodory scales into the “unit scale” in an appropriately uniform way. In Section 2.1 we describe what we mean by the unit scale and in Section 2.2 we state the main scaling result. The scaling maps defined here have their roots in the influential paper of Nagel, Stein, and Wainger [NSW85] for manifolds without boundary. The work in [Str25a] builds on the results of [SS18], which in turn draw on ideas of Nagel, Stein, and Wainger [NSW85] and of Tao and Wright [TW03].

This section is somewhat technical, and on a first reading, the reader may find it helpful to skip this section and refer back to it as needed.

2.1 The unit scale

The main scaling result (Theorem 2.4) allows us to rescale Hörmander vector fields at a small scale, so that they are Hörmander vector fields at the unit scale “uniformly” in various parameters. This uniformity is explained here.

Define ℝ≥n:={(x′,xn)∈ℝn−1×ℝ:xn≥0}\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}:=\left\{(x^{\prime},x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}:x_{n}\geq 0\right\}. Let UU be an open subset of either ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} or ℝ≥n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}, where the latter carries its usual topology as a subspace of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. For L∈ℤ≥={0,1,2,…}L\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}=\left\{0,1,2,\ldots\right\}, set

CbL​(U):={f∈CL​(U):∂xαf​ is bounded ​∀|α|≤L},C_{b}^{L}(U):=\left\{f\in C^{L}(U):\partial_{x}^{\alpha}f\text{ is bounded }\forall|\alpha|\leq L\right\},
‖f‖CbL​(U):=supx∈Umax|α|≤L⁡|∂xαf⁡(x)|.\|f\|_{C_{b}^{L}(U)}:=\sup_{x\in U}\max_{|\alpha|\leq L}\left|\partial_{x}^{\alpha}f(x)\right|.

Set Cb∞​(U):=⋂LCbL​(U)C_{b}^{\infty}(U):=\bigcap_{L}C_{b}^{L}(U), endowed with the usual Fréchet topology. We similarly define the vector-valued analogs CbL​(U,ℝk)C_{b}^{L}(U;\mathbb{R}^{k}) and Cb∞​(U,ℝk)C_{b}^{\infty}(U;\mathbb{R}^{k}).

For a smooth vector field XX on UU, we write XX with respect to the standard basis X(x)=∑aj(x)∂xjX(x)=\sum a_{j}(x)\partial_{x_{j}}, and identify XX with the function x↦(a1​(x),…,an​(x))∈C∞​(U,ℝn)x\mapsto\left(a_{1}(x),\ldots,a_{n}(x)\right)\in C^{\infty}(U;\mathbb{R}^{n}). It therefore makes sense to ask whether X∈Cb∞​(U,ℝn)X\in C_{b}^{\infty}(U;\mathbb{R}^{n}).

Definition 2.1.

Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be an index set, and for ι∈ℐ\iota\in\mathcal{I} let X1ι,…,Xqιι∈Cb∞​(U,ℝn)X_{1}^{\iota},\ldots,X_{q_{\iota}}^{\iota}\in C_{b}^{\infty}(U;\mathbb{R}^{n}) be smooth vector fields on UU. We say X1ι,…,XqιιX_{1}^{\iota},\ldots,X_{q_{\iota}}^{\iota} span the tangent space to UU, uniformly for ι∈ℐ\iota\in\mathcal{I} if

infι∈ℐinfx∈Umaxj1,…,jn∈{1,…,qι}⁡|det(Xj1ι​(x)|Xj2ι​(x)​|⋯|​Xjnι​(x))|>0,\inf_{\iota\in\mathcal{I}}\inf_{x\in U}\max_{j_{1},\ldots,j_{n}\in\left\{1,\ldots,q_{\iota}\right\}}\left|\det\left(X_{j_{1}}^{\iota}(x)|X_{j_{2}}^{\iota}(x)|\cdots|X_{j_{n}}^{\iota}(x)\right)\right|>0,

where (Xj1ι​(x)|Xj2ι​(x)​|⋯|​Xjnι​(x))\left(X_{j_{1}}^{\iota}(x)|X_{j_{2}}^{\iota}(x)|\cdots|X_{j_{n}}^{\iota}(x)\right) is the n×nn\times n matrix whose kk-th column is Xjkι​(x)X_{j_{k}}^{\iota}(x) written as a column vector.

Definition 2.2.

Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be an index set, and for ι∈ℐ\iota\in\mathcal{I} let W1ι,…,Wrιι∈Cb∞​(U,ℝn)W_{1}^{\iota},\ldots,W_{r_{\iota}}^{\iota}\in C_{b}^{\infty}(U;\mathbb{R}^{n}) be smooth vector fields on UU. We say that W1ι,…,WrιιW_{1}^{\iota},\ldots,W_{r_{\iota}}^{\iota} are Hörmander vector fields on UU, uniformly for ι∈ℐ\iota\in\mathcal{I} if the following conditions hold:

  • •

    supι∈ℐrι<∞\sup_{\iota\in\mathcal{I}}r_{\iota}<\infty.

  • •

    {Wjι:ι∈ℐ,1≤j≤rι}⊆Cb∞(U;ℝn)\left\{W_{j}^{\iota}:\iota\in\mathcal{I},1\leq j\leq r_{\iota}\right\}\subseteq C_{b}^{\infty}(U;\mathbb{R}^{n}) is a bounded set.

  • •

    ∃m∈ℤ>\exists m\in\mathbb{Z}_{>} (independent of ι\iota) such that if X1ι,…,XqιιX_{1}^{\iota},\ldots,X_{q_{\iota}}^{\iota} is an enumeration of the commutators of W1ι,…,WrιιW_{1}^{\iota},\ldots,W_{r_{\iota}}^{\iota} up to order mm, then X1ι,…,XqιιX_{1}^{\iota},\ldots,X_{q_{\iota}}^{\iota} span the tangent space to UU, uniformly for ι∈ℐ\iota\in\mathcal{I} (see Definition 2.1).

Remark 2.3.

The main point of Definition 2.2 is that the subelliptic estimates used below hold uniformly under suitable uniform hypotheses; a key such hypothesis is that the vector fields are uniformly Hörmander in the sense of Definition 2.2.

2.2 The scaling result

Let 𝔑\mathfrak{N} be a smooth manifold with boundary of dimension n≥2n\geq 2, and let Vol\mathrm{Vol} be a smooth strictly positive density on 𝔑\mathfrak{N}. Let W1,…,WrW_{1},\ldots,W_{r} be Hörmander vector fields on a manifold with boundary 𝔑\mathfrak{N}. That is, W1,…,WrW_{1},\ldots,W_{r} are smooth vector fields on 𝔑\mathfrak{N} satisfying Hörmander’s condition: the Lie algebra generated by W1,…,WrW_{1},\ldots,W_{r} spans the tangent space at every point. and V=(V0,V1,…,Vr)V=(V_{0},V_{1},\ldots,V_{r}). Let BW​(ξ,δ)B_{W}(\xi,\delta) and BV​(ξ,δ)B_{V}(\xi,\delta) be as in (1.3), and let ρW\rho_{W} and ρV\rho_{V} be as in (1.4).

2.3 Proof of Theorem 2.4

In this section, we present the proof of Theorem 2.4. The result is largely contained in [Str25a], so it is merely a matter of translating the results there into the setting we require. The reader wishing to follow the proof should have a copy of [Str25a] at hand.

For 1 and 2, we use [Str25a, Theorems and ]. Indeed, we take 𝔑\mathfrak{N} in those theorems to be 𝔑1\mathfrak{N}_{1} and (W,d)={(W1,1),…,(Wr,1)}(W,d)=\left\{(W_{1},1),\ldots,(W_{r},1)\right\}. With these choices, every point of ∂𝔑1\partial\mathfrak{N}_{1} is (W,d)(W,d)-non-characteristic (see [Str25a, Definition ]) since it is WW-non-characteristic by the choice of XX and 𝔑1\mathfrak{N}_{1}. In short, 𝔑(W,d)nc\mathfrak{N}_{(W,d)}^{\mathrm{nc}} from [Str25a, Theorem ] equals 𝔑1\mathfrak{N}_{1}. From here, 1 for WW follows immediately from [Str25a, Theorem ]. The same proof, with WW replaced by VV, gives the same result for VV.

For 2, we set (Z,d​~)={(V0,1),(V1,1),…,(Vr,1)}(Z,{d\hskip-0.80002pt\widetilde{}\hskip 1.00006pt})=\left\{(V_{0},1),(V_{1},1),\ldots,(V_{r},1)\right\}. The construction of VV implies (W,d)(W,d) and (Z,d​~)(Z,{d\hskip-0.80002pt\widetilde{}\hskip 1.00006pt}) are locally strongly equivalent and hence locally weakly equivalent in the sense of [Str25a, Definition ]. 3 The main technical theorem

In this section, we present the main technical result of this paper. The statement is somewhat involved because our goal is to formulate the result using only the assumptions needed for the proof. For more accessible corollaries, we refer the reader to Corollary 1.4 and Section 4.

Let 𝔑\mathfrak{N} be a smooth manifold with boundary with n≔dim⁡(𝔑)≥2n\coloneqq\Dimension(\mathfrak{N})\geq 2, let Vol\mathrm{Vol} be a smooth, strictly positive density on 𝔑\mathfrak{N}, and fix M∈ℤ>M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>}. Let (𝒬,Dom⁡(𝒬))(\mathcal{Q},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})) be a closed, densely defined, sesquilinear form on L2​(𝔑,Vol,ℂM)L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol};\mathbb{C}^{M}) which is sectorial with vertex γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathbb{R}; see [Kat95, Sections 1.1-1.3] for the relevant definitions. We recall that (𝒬,Dom⁡(𝒬))(\mathcal{Q},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})) is called sectorial with vertex γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathbb{R}, which may be negative, if ∃C≥0\exists C\geq 0,

γ​‖f‖L22≤Re⁡𝒬⁡(f,f),|Im⁡𝒬⁡(f,f)|≤C⁡(Re⁡𝒬⁡(f,f)−γ​‖f‖L22),∀f∈Dom⁡(𝒬).\gamma\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\Real\mathcal{Q}(f,f),\quad\left|\Imaginary\mathcal{Q}(f,f)\right|\leq C\left(\Real\mathcal{Q}(f,f)-\gamma\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\right),\quad\forall f\in\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}). (3.1)

By [Kat95, Chapter 6, Theorem 2.1], there is a unique, closed, densely defined, m-sectorial operator (with vertex γ\gamma) associated with (𝒬,Dom⁡(𝒬))(\mathcal{Q},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})), which we denote by (ℒ,Dom⁡(ℒ))(\mathscr{L},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})). It is the maximal operator satisfying (1.2); see [Kat95, Chapter 6, Theorem 2.1] for details.

Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}) can be given the structure of a Hilbert space by defining

‖f‖Dom⁡(𝒬)2=Re⁡𝒬⁡(f,f)+Γ​‖f‖L22,\|f\|_{\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})}^{2}=\Real\mathcal{Q}(f,f)+\Gamma\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}, (3.2)

where Γ≫1\Gamma\gg 1 is sufficiently large (any two such choices of Γ\Gamma yield equivalent norms). We henceforth equip Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}) with this topology. Since ℒ\mathscr{L} is a closed operator, Dom⁡(ℒ)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L}) is a Banach space with the graph norm ‖f‖L2+‖ℒ​f‖L2\|f\|_{L^{2}}+\|\mathscr{L}f\|_{L^{2}}; we equip Dom⁡(ℒ)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L}) with the corresponding topology and treat Dom⁡(ℒ∗)\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right) similarly.

Lemma 3.1.

(−ℒ,Dom⁡(ℒ))(-\mathscr{L},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})) is the generator of a strongly continuous semigroup T⁡(t)=e−t​ℒ:L2​(𝔑,Vol,ℂM)→L2​(𝔑,Vol,ℂM)T(t)=e^{-t\mathscr{L}}:L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol};\mathbb{C}^{M})\rightarrow L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol};\mathbb{C}^{M}) which satisfies ‖T⁡(t)‖L2→L2≤e−γ​t\|T(t)\|_{L^{2}\rightarrow L^{2}}\leq e^{-\gamma t}, ∀t≥0\forall t\geq 0.

Proof.

This uses only the fact that (ℒ,Dom⁡(ℒ))(\mathscr{L},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})) is an m-sectorial operator with vertex γ\gamma. Indeed, the definition of m-sectoriality with vertex γ\gamma (see [Kat95, Chapter 5, Section 3.10]) implies that (ℒ−γ,Dom⁡(ℒ))\left(\mathscr{L}-\gamma,\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})\right) is m-accretive. The result then follows from the Lumer–Phillips theorem [EN06, Chapter 2, Theorem 3.15].

Moreover, [Kat95, Chapter 9, Section 1, Theorem 1.24] shows that T⁡(t)T(t) is a holomorphic semigroup, though we do not use this fact. ∎

Fix κ∈ℤ>\kappa\in\mathbb{Z}_{>}. For U~⊆𝔑0\widetilde{U}\subseteq\mathfrak{N}_{0} open, define

HWκ(U~;ℂM):={f∈L2(U~,Vol;ℂM):Wαf∈L2(U~,Vol;ℂM),∀|α|≤κ},H^{\kappa}_{W}(\widetilde{U};\mathbb{C}^{M}):=\left\{f\in L^{2}(\widetilde{U},\mathrm{Vol};\mathbb{C}^{M}):W^{\alpha}f\in L^{2}(\widetilde{U},\mathrm{Vol};\mathbb{C}^{M}),\>\forall|\alpha|\leq\kappa\right\}, (3.3)

and give HW,locκ​(U~,ℂM)H^{\kappa}_{W,\mathrm{loc}}(\widetilde{U};\mathbb{C}^{M}) the usual Fréchet topology.

For lists α,β\alpha,\beta of elements of {1,…,r}\left\{1,\ldots,r\right\}, with |α|,|β|≤κ|\alpha|,|\beta|\leq\kappa, let aα,β∈C∞​(Ω1,𝕄M×M​(ℂ))a_{\alpha,\beta}\in C^{\infty}(\Omega_{1};\mathbb{M}^{M\times M}(\mathbb{C})). Define

Here, “F” stands for “formula” because 𝒬F\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{F}} provides a formula for 𝒬\mathcal{Q} (see Assumption 3.5).

The following assumptions are very similar to those in [Str26, Section 3]; indeed, the results of that paper play a key role in the proof of Theorem 3.14.

Assumption 3.2.

The map f↦f|Ωf\mapsto f\big|_{\Omega} maps Dom⁡(𝒬)→HW,locκ​(Ω,ℂM)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})\rightarrow H^{\kappa}_{W,\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{M}) (we do not assume continuity).

Remark 3.3.

The map in Assumption 3.2 is automatically continuous. Indeed, it has closed graph: if fj→ff_{j}\rightarrow f in Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}) and fj|Ω→gf_{j}\big|_{\Omega}\rightarrow g in HW,locκ​(Ω,ℂM)H^{\kappa}_{W,\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{M}), then these convergences imply fj|Ω→f|Ωf_{j}\big|_{\Omega}\rightarrow f\big|_{\Omega} and fj|Ω→gf_{j}\big|_{\Omega}\rightarrow g in Lloc2L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}. It follows that f|Ω=gf\big|_{\Omega}=g and therefore the graph is closed. The closed graph theorem implies the map is continuous.

Remark 3.4.

Assumption 3.2 is the “maximally subelliptic” estimate. Indeed, given a compact set 𝒦2⋐Ω\mathcal{K}_{2}\Subset\Omega, Remark 3.3 implies that there exists C𝒦2≥0C_{\mathcal{K}_{2}}\geq 0 such that ∀f∈Dom⁡(𝒬)\forall f\in\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}) with supp⁡(f)⊆𝒦2\supp(f)\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{2}, we have

‖f‖HWκ2≤C𝒦2​(|𝒬⁡(f,f)|+‖f‖L22).\|f\|_{H^{\kappa}_{W}}^{2}\leq C_{\mathcal{K}_{2}}\left(\left|\mathcal{Q}(f,f)\right|+\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\right). (3.5)
Assumption 3.5.

∀f,g∈Dom⁡(𝒬)\forall f,g\in\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}), with supp⁡(f)⊆Ω\supp(f)\subseteq\Omega or supp⁡(g)⊆Ω\supp(g)\subseteq\Omega, 𝒬⁡(f,g)=𝒬F​(f,g)\mathcal{Q}(f,g)=\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{F}}(f,g).

Assumption 3.6.

𝒟0​(𝔑,ℂM)⊆Dom⁡(ℒ)∩Dom⁡(ℒ∗)\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{C}^{M})\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})\cap\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right). Moreover, there is a partial differential operator ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} with smooth 𝕄M×M​(ℂ)\mathbb{M}^{M\times M}(\mathbb{C})-valued coefficients such that

ℒ​f=ℒ0​f,∀f∈𝒟0​(𝔑,ℂM).\mathscr{L}f=\mathscr{L}_{0}f,\quad\forall f\in\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{C}^{M}). (3.6)
Remark 3.7.

Assumption 3.6 is symmetric in ℒ\mathscr{L} and ℒ∗\mathscr{L}^{*}. Indeed, the density of 𝒟0​(𝔑,ℂM)\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{C}^{M}) in L2​(𝔑,Vol,ℂM)L^{2}\left(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol};\mathbb{C}^{M}\right) combined with (3.6) implies

ℒ∗​f=ℒ0∗​f,∀f∈𝒟0​(𝔑,ℂM),\mathscr{L}^{*}f=\mathscr{L}_{0}^{*}f,\quad\forall f\in\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{C}^{M}),

Assumption 3.6 combined with Remark 3.4 gives the interior maximally subelliptic estimates. Namely, we have 𝒟0​(U,ℂM)⊆Dom⁡(ℒ)⊆Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathscr{D}_{0}(U;\mathbb{C}^{M})\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}), by Assumption 3.6. Using that U¯⋐Ω\overline{U}\Subset\Omega, Remark 3.4 shows ∃C0≥0\exists C_{0}\geq 0, ∀f∈𝒟0​(U,ℂM)\forall f\in\mathscr{D}_{0}(U;\mathbb{C}^{M}),

‖f‖HWκ2≤C0​(|𝒬⁡(f,f)|+‖f‖L22).\|f\|_{H^{\kappa}_{W}}^{2}\leq C_{0}\left(\left|\mathcal{Q}(f,f)\right|+\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\right).

If g∈Dom⁡(ℒ)g\in\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L}), then by Assumption 3.5,

⟨f,ℒ​g⟩L2=𝒬⁡(f,g)=𝒬F​(f,g),∀f∈Dom⁡(𝒬)​ with ​supp⁡(f)⊆Ω.\langle f,\mathscr{L}g\rangle_{L^{2}}=\mathcal{Q}(f,g)=\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{F}}(f,g),\quad\forall f\in\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})\text{ with }\supp(f)\subseteq\Omega.

ℒ​g|Ω=∑|α|,|β|≤κ(Wα)∗​aα,β​Wβ​g|Ω,\mathscr{L}g\big|_{\Omega}=\sum_{|\alpha|,|\beta|\leq\kappa}\left(W^{\alpha}\right)^{*}a_{\alpha,\beta}W^{\beta}g\big|_{\Omega}, (3.7)

Remark 3.10.

Assumption 3.6 is often immediate in applications. Indeed, if Assumption 3.5 holds with Ω\Omega replaced by 𝔑\mathfrak{N} and 𝒟0​(𝔑,ℂM)⊆Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{C}^{M})\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}), then Assumption 3.6 follows. However, imposing Assumption 3.5 only on Ω\Omega allows us to prove results that apply even when no globally defined Hörmander vector fields define 𝒬\mathcal{Q}: we need such vector fields only in a neighborhood of the region where we wish to estimate the heat kernel.

Our final assumption, inspired by the work of Kohn and Nirenberg [KN65], plays a key role in the a priori estimates developed in [Str26]. It says that smoothing in the tangential and time variables preserves the form boundary conditions; combined with Assumption 3.2 this gives tangentially regularized maximally subelliptic estimates (see Lemma 3.15). We use the half-cube Q≥n​(δ′)Q^{n}_{\geq}(\delta^{\prime}) and the cube Qn−1​(δ′)Q^{n-1}(\delta^{\prime}) from Section 2.2. Remark 3.12.

In Assumption 3.11, we impose conditions on both Dom⁡(ℒ)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L}) and Dom⁡(ℒ∗)\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right). One can simplify the formulation by replacing both with the larger space Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}). Because Dom⁡(ℒ)↪Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}) and Dom⁡(ℒ∗)↪Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right)\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}), this stronger assumption is automatically symmetric in (ℒ,Dom⁡(ℒ))(\mathscr{L},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})) and (ℒ∗,Dom⁡(ℒ∗))\left(\mathscr{L}^{*},\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right)\right). It is often easier to verify assumptions on a core for (𝒬,Dom⁡(𝒬))(\mathcal{Q},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})) than on all of Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}). See Section 4 for a result in which we use assumptions only on the core.

continuously. ‖Tξ,δ​u​(t,⋅)‖HWκ2≤A⁡(|𝒬⁡(Tξ,δ​u​(t,⋅),Tξ,δ​u​(t,⋅))|+‖Tξ,δ​u​(t,⋅)‖L2​(𝔑,d​Vol)2).\left\|T_{\xi,\delta}u(t,\cdot)\right\|_{H^{\kappa}_{W}}^{2}\leq A\left(\left|\mathcal{Q}\left(T_{\xi,\delta}u(t,\cdot),T_{\xi,\delta}u(t,\cdot)\right)\right|+\left\|T_{\xi,\delta}u(t,\cdot)\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N};d\mathrm{Vol})}^{2}\right).

Remark 3.16.

The assumptions of this section are symmetric in (ℒ,Dom⁡(ℒ))(\mathscr{L},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})) and (ℒ∗,Dom⁡(ℒ∗))\left(\mathscr{L}^{*},\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right)\right) because (ℒ∗,Dom⁡(ℒ∗))\left(\mathscr{L}^{*},\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right)\right) corresponds to the form (𝒬∗,Dom⁡(𝒬))(\mathcal{Q}^{*},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})); see Remark 3.12. Thus, Theorem 3.14 also holds with (ℒ,Dom⁡(ℒ))(\mathscr{L},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})) replaced by (ℒ∗,Dom⁡(ℒ∗))\left(\mathscr{L}^{*},\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right)\right). Notably, (−ℒ∗,Dom⁡(ℒ∗))\left(-\mathscr{L}^{*},\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right)\right) is the generator of the strongly continuous semigroup T​(t)∗T(t)^{*}; see [EN06, Chapter 2, Section 2.5].

4 A core criterion for the Gaussian bounds

Section 3 imposes a number of assumptions on (𝒬,Dom⁡(𝒬))(\mathcal{Q},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})) that involve all of Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}). Often, however, (𝒬,Dom⁡(𝒬))(\mathcal{Q},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})) is initially defined on a core, or the relevant properties are easier to verify on a core (usually a space of smooth functions). In this section, we present Corollary 4.7, a corollary of Theorem 3.14 in which the relevant assumptions are imposed on a core. The results here closely follow similar results in [Str26, Section ].

As in Section 3, let 𝔑\mathfrak{N} be a smooth manifold with boundary, with n≔dim⁡(𝔑)≥2n\coloneqq\Dimension(\mathfrak{N})\geq 2, let Vol\mathrm{Vol} be a smooth, strictly positive density on 𝔑\mathfrak{N}, and fix M∈ℤ>M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>}. Let (𝒬,Dom⁡(𝒬))(\mathcal{Q},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})) be a closed, densely defined, sectorial sesquilinear form on L2​(𝔑,Vol,ℂM)L^{2}\left(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol};\mathbb{C}^{M}\right). Let (ℒ,Dom⁡(ℒ))(\mathscr{L},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})) be the unique, closed, densely defined, m-sectorial operator on L2​(𝔑,Vol,ℂM)L^{2}\left(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol};\mathbb{C}^{M}\right) associated with (𝒬,Dom⁡(𝒬))(\mathcal{Q},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})) (see Section 3 for details).

Let 𝔑0⊆𝔑\mathfrak{N}_{0}\subseteq\mathfrak{N} be an open set and let W1,…,WrW_{1},\ldots,W_{r} be Hörmander vector fields on 𝔑0\mathfrak{N}_{0}. Fix XX in the C∞​(𝔑0,ℝ)C^{\infty}(\mathfrak{N}_{0};\mathbb{R}) module generated by W1,…,WrW_{1},\ldots,W_{r} and let 𝔑1⊆𝔑0\mathfrak{N}_{1}\subseteq\mathfrak{N}_{0} be an open set such that ∀ξ∈∂𝔑1=𝔑1∩∂𝔑\forall\xi\in\partial\mathfrak{N}_{1}=\mathfrak{N}_{1}\cap\partial\mathfrak{N}, X⁡(ξ)∉Tξ​∂𝔑X(\xi)\not\in T_{\xi}\partial\mathfrak{N}. Let V0,V1,…,VrV_{0},V_{1},\ldots,V_{r} be as in Section 2.2 with this choice of XX and 𝔑1\mathfrak{N}_{1}.

Fix an open, relatively compact set U⋐𝔑1U\Subset\mathfrak{N}_{1} and set 𝒦1:=U¯⋐𝔑1\mathcal{K}_{1}:=\overline{U}\Subset\mathfrak{N}_{1}. Fix an open, relatively compact set Ω⋐𝔑1\Omega\Subset\mathfrak{N}_{1}, with 𝒦1⋐Ω\mathcal{K}_{1}\Subset\Omega. Let 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}, 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}, Φξ,δ\Phi_{\xi,\delta}, Ψξ,δ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}, and δ1∈(0,1]\delta_{1}\in(0,1] be as in Theorem 2.4 with the above choices.

For lists α,β\alpha,\beta of elements of {1,…,r}\left\{1,\ldots,r\right\}, with |α|,|β|≤κ|\alpha|,|\beta|\leq\kappa, let aα,β∈C∞​(𝔑0,𝕄M×M​(ℂ))a_{\alpha,\beta}\in C^{\infty}(\mathfrak{N}_{0};\mathbb{M}^{M\times M}(\mathbb{C})). Define 𝒬F\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{F}} as in (3.4).

Let ℬ⊆Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathscr{B}\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}) be a core for (𝒬,Dom⁡(𝒬))(\mathcal{Q},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q})) (see [Kat95, Chapter 6, Section 1.4]).

Assumption 4.1.

There exist ψ∈Ccpt∞​(𝔑0,ℝ)\psi\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}(\mathfrak{N}_{0};\mathbb{R}) with ψ=1\psi=1 on a neighborhood of Ω¯\overline{\Omega} and C1≥0C_{1}\geq 0 such that the map f↦ψ​ff\mapsto\psi f sends ℬ→ℬ\mathscr{B}\rightarrow\mathscr{B} and satisfies

For functions K⁡(x,y′)∈Ccpt∞​(Q≥n​(1/2)×Qn−1​(1/2))K(x,y^{\prime})\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}\left(Q^{n}_{\geq}(1/2)\times Q^{n-1}(1/2)\right) such that ∃δ′>0\exists\delta^{\prime}>0 with ∂xnK⁡((x′,xn),y′)=0\partial_{x_{n}}K((x^{\prime},x_{n}),y^{\prime})=0 for 0≤xn<δ′0\leq x_{n}<\delta^{\prime}, we consider operators of the form

Assumption 4.5.

∀(ξ,δ)∈𝒮2\forall(\xi,\delta)\in\mathcal{S}_{2}, for all operators SS of the form (4.1) (for any δ′>0\delta^{\prime}>0), set Tξ,δ:=(Ψξ,δ)∗​S​Ψξ,δ∗T_{\xi,\delta}:=\left(\Psi_{\xi,\delta}\right)_{*}S\Psi_{\xi,\delta}^{*} as in Assumption 3.11. Then, Tξ,δ:ℬ→Dom⁡(𝒬)T_{\xi,\delta}:\mathscr{B}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}).

To verify Assumption 4.5, it is often easier to show Tξ,δ:ℬ→ℬT_{\xi,\delta}:\mathscr{B}\rightarrow\mathscr{B}. This is stronger, since ℬ⊆Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathscr{B}\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}).

Corollary 4.7.

Under the above assumptions, the conclusions of Theorem 3.14 hold.

Corollary 4.7 follows immediately from the next proposition.

Proposition 4.8.

Under the above assumptions, the assumptions of Section 3 hold.

The proof of Proposition 4.8 closely follows the proof of [Str26, Proposition ]. Thus, we outline the proof here and describe only the changes needed to adapt it to the setting of this paper.

  1. 1.

Lemma 4.11.

Let K⁡(x,y′)∈Ccpt∞​(Q≥n​(1/2)×Qn−1​(1/2))K(x,y^{\prime})\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}(Q^{n}_{\geq}(1/2)\times Q^{n-1}(1/2)) and for (ξ,δ)∈𝒮2(\xi,\delta)\in\mathcal{S}_{2}, set

Proof.

Fix (ξ,δ)∈𝒮2(\xi,\delta)\in\mathcal{S}_{2}. In what follows, the constants in the estimates are allowed to depend on (ξ,δ)(\xi,\delta). Let XX be as in the beginning of this section. We will show

∑|α|≤κ‖Wα​Tξ,δ​f‖L2≲∑j=0κ‖Xj​f‖L2​(Ψξ,δ​(Q≥n​(1/2))).\sum_{|\alpha|\leq\kappa}\left\|W^{\alpha}T_{\xi,\delta}f\right\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\sum_{j=0}^{\kappa}\left\|X^{j}f\right\|_{L^{2}(\Psi_{\xi,\delta}(Q^{n}_{\geq}(1/2)))}. (4.3)

To see why (4.3) completes the proof, note supp⁡(Tξ,δ​f)⊆Ψξ,δ​(Q≥n​(1/2))⊆BV​(ξ,δ)⊆Ω\supp(T_{\xi,\delta}f)\subseteq\Psi_{\xi,\delta}(Q^{n}_{\geq}(1/2))\subseteq B_{V}(\xi,\delta)\subseteq\Omega, where we have used Theorem 2.47. (4.3) gives

‖Tξ,δ​f‖HWκ=∑|α|≤κ‖Wα​Tξ,δ​f‖L2≲∑j=0κ‖Xj​f‖L2​(Ψξ,δ​(Q≥n​(1/2)))≲∑|α|≤κ‖Wα​f‖L2​(𝔑0)=‖f‖HWκ​(𝔑0),\left\|T_{\xi,\delta}f\right\|_{H^{\kappa}_{W}}=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq\kappa}\left\|W^{\alpha}T_{\xi,\delta}f\right\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\sum_{j=0}^{\kappa}\left\|X^{j}f\right\|_{L^{2}(\Psi_{\xi,\delta}(Q^{n}_{\geq}(1/2)))}\lesssim\sum_{|\alpha|\leq\kappa}\left\|W^{\alpha}f\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N}_{0})}=\|f\|_{H^{\kappa}_{W}(\mathfrak{N}_{0})},

establishing the result.

We turn to proving (4.3). Since Vol\mathrm{Vol} is a smooth, strictly positive density on 𝔑\mathfrak{N} and Ψξ,δ​(Q≥n​(1/2))⋐𝔑\Psi_{\xi,\delta}(Q^{n}_{\geq}(1/2))\Subset\mathfrak{N} (see Theorem 2.47), we have

5 Proof of Theorem 3.14

In this section, we present the proof of Theorem 3.14. The proof uses the estimates of [Str26] to verify the hypotheses of [Str25c, Theorem ], which in turn yields the result. Both [Str26] and [Str25c] were written with this paper in mind, and we can use those papers with only minor modifications to establish Theorem 3.14. The reader who wishes to follow the proof should have both references at hand.

The heart of the proof is to use the subelliptic estimates of [Str26] combined with the scaling from Theorem 2.4 to establish an appropriate subelliptic estimate at every scale for heat operators like ∂t+ℒ\partial_{t}+\mathscr{L}, “uniformly over every scale.” As a consequence, we obtain hypoelliptic estimates uniformly over every scale, which is the main hypothesis of [Str25c, Theorem ]. The conclusion of [Str25c, Theorem ] then gives the desired higher-order Gaussian bounds.

Throughout this section, we take the same setting and assume all the assumptions from Section 3.

5.1 Subellipticity and qualitative consequences

Before we move to the key quantitative parts of the proof, we discuss some qualitative consequences of the subelliptic estimates in [Str26].

We first remark that the assumptions of [Str26, Section ] hold with Ω\Omega in that reference replaced by UU. Indeed, [Str26, Assumption ] follows from Assumption 3.6 and Dom⁡(ℒ)⊆Dom⁡(𝒬)\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}) and since U⊆ΩU\subseteq\Omega (where Ω\Omega is as in Section 3), [Str26, Assumption ] follows from Assumption 3.2, and [Str26, Assumption ] follows immediately from Assumption 3.5. Indeed, they are almost verbatim copies. All that remains is [Str26, Assumption ]. Take ξ0∈U∩∂𝔑⊆𝒦1\xi_{0}\in U\cap\partial\mathfrak{N}\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{1}. Since ρV\rho_{V} induces the manifold topology on 𝔑1\mathfrak{N}_{1}, choose δ⁡(ξ0)∈(0,δ1]\delta(\xi_{0})\in(0,\delta_{1}] sufficiently small that BV​(ξ0,δ⁡(ξ0)/2)⊆UB_{V}(\xi_{0},\delta(\xi_{0})/2)\subseteq U. By Theorem 2.412, Ψξ0,δ⁡(ξ0)∗X=±δ(ξ0)−1D∂xn\Psi_{\xi_{0},\delta(\xi_{0})}^{*}X=\pm\delta(\xi_{0})^{-1}D\partial_{x_{n}}, and therefore Ψξ0,δ⁡(ξ0)∗X=c1∂xn\Psi_{\xi_{0},\delta(\xi_{0})}^{*}X=c_{1}\partial_{x_{n}}, where c1c_{1} is a constant. Since ξ0∈∂𝔑\xi_{0}\in\partial\mathfrak{N}, Theorem 2.49 shows Ψξ0,δ⁡(ξ0)​(0)=ξ0\Psi_{\xi_{0},\delta(\xi_{0})}(0)=\xi_{0}. With these comments, [Str26, Assumption ] (with x0x_{0} replaced by ξ0\xi_{0}) follows directly from Assumption 3.11 with Ψ=Ψξ0,δ⁡(ξ0)\Psi=\Psi_{\xi_{0},\delta(\xi_{0})}. Indeed, [Str26, Assumption ] follows from Ψξ0,δ⁡(ξ0)∗X=c1∂xn\Psi_{\xi_{0},\delta(\xi_{0})}^{*}X=c_{1}\partial_{x_{n}}, while [Str26, Assumption ] is a copy of Assumption 3.11.

Thus, the results from [Str26, Section ] hold for (ℒ,Dom⁡(ℒ))(\mathscr{L},\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})). From here, (5.3) for ℒ\mathscr{L} follows from the Sobolev Embedding Theorem, by taking l=l⁡(L)l=l(L) large, and moreover ϕ1​u∈C∞​(I×V,ℂM)\phi_{1}u\in C^{\infty}(I\times V;\mathbb{C}^{M}). As ϕ1∈Ccpt∞​(I×V)\phi_{1}\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}(I\times V) was arbitrary, we conclude u∈C∞​(I×V,ℂM)u\in C^{\infty}(I\times V;\mathbb{C}^{M}). The same proof applies for ℒ∗\mathscr{L}^{*}. ∎

For the next lemma, we consider the space Dom⁡(ℒ∞)=⋂j∈ℤ>Dom⁡(ℒj)\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{\infty}\right)=\bigcap_{j\in\mathbb{Z}_{>}}\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{j}\right). This is a Fréchet space because −ℒ-\mathscr{L} generates a strongly continuous semigroup by Lemma 3.1 and therefore has a nonempty resolvent set. Indeed, for each mm, Dom⁡(ℒm)=⋂j=1mDom⁡(ℒj)\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{m}\right)=\bigcap_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{j}\right), equipped with the norm ∑j=0m‖ℒj​f‖L2\sum_{j=0}^{m}\left\|\mathscr{L}^{j}f\right\|_{L^{2}}, is a Banach space by [EN06, Chapter 2, Proposition 2.15]; the claim that Dom⁡(ℒ∞)\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{\infty}\right) is a Fréchet space follows immediately.

Lemma 5.3.

The map f↦f|Uf\mapsto f\big|_{U} is continuous Dom⁡(ℒ∞)→C∞​(U,ℂM)\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{\infty}\right)\rightarrow C^{\infty}\left(U;\mathbb{C}^{M}\right). The same is true for ℒ\mathscr{L} replaced by ℒ∗\mathscr{L}^{*}.

Proof.

For ℒ\mathscr{L}, this follows immediately from [Str26, Corollary ]. Since our assumptions are symmetric in ℒ\mathscr{L} and ℒ∗\mathscr{L}^{*} (see Remark 3.16), the result follows for ℒ∗\mathscr{L}^{*} as well. ∎

Finally, we show the existence of the smooth kernel as in (3.9). We begin with a lemma. For it, we write Lw2L^{2}_{w} for L2L^{2} equipped with the weak topology.

supt,ξ‖𝒫⁡(ϕ⁡(t,ξ)​Kt​(ξ,⋅))‖L2​(𝔑,Vol)<∞.\sup_{t,\xi}\left\|\mathscr{P}\left(\phi(t,\xi)K_{t}(\xi,\cdot)\right)\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}<\infty. (5.4)

For f∈Dom⁡(ℒ)f\in\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}\right), we have

(∂t+ℒ)T(t)f=0\left(\partial_{t}+\mathscr{L}\right)T(t)f=0 (5.5)

(see [EN06, Chapter 2, Lemma 1.3(ii)]).

Fix ϕ1,ϕ2∈Ccpt∞​((0,∞)×U)\phi_{1},\phi_{2}\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}((0,\infty)\times U) with ϕ1≺ϕ2\phi_{1}\prec\phi_{2}. The next lemma is standard, though we include the proof for completeness.

Lemma 5.5.

Suppose M⁡(t,x,y)∈L2​(ℝ×ℝ≥n×ℝ≥n)M(t,x,y)\in L^{2}\left(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}\right) is such that ∀j\forall j, ∀α\forall\alpha,

∂tjM⁡(t,x,y),∂xαM⁡(t,x,y),∂yαM⁡(t,x,y)∈L2​(ℝ×ℝ≥n×ℝ≥n).\partial_{t}^{j}M(t,x,y),\partial_{x}^{\alpha}M(t,x,y),\partial_{y}^{\alpha}M(t,x,y)\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}). (5.7)

Then M⁡(t,x,y)∈C∞​(ℝ×ℝ≥n×ℝ≥n)M(t,x,y)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}).

Proof.

Let ℰ\mathscr{E} be the extension operator constructed by Seeley in [See64] that maps functions on [0,∞)[0,\infty) to functions on ℝ\mathbb{R}. We treat ℰ\mathscr{E} as an operator acting only in the last variable of ℝ≥n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}. Thus, ℰ​f|ℝ≥n=f\mathscr{E}f\big|_{\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}}=f and for every Hilbert space ℋ\mathscr{H} and every m∈ℤ≥m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}, ℰ\mathscr{E} extends to a bounded map

ℰ:Hm​(ℝ≥n,ℋ)→Hm​(ℝn,ℋ).\mathscr{E}:H^{m}(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq};\mathscr{H})\rightarrow H^{m}(\mathbb{R}^{n};\mathscr{H}). (5.8)

Let ℰx\mathscr{E}_{x} and ℰy\mathscr{E}_{y} denote this extension operator acting in the xx and yy variables, respectively, and define M~(t,⋅x,⋅y)≔ℰyℰxM(t,⋅x,⋅y)\widetilde{M}(t,\cdot_{x},\cdot_{y})\coloneqq\mathscr{E}_{y}\mathscr{E}_{x}M(t,\cdot_{x},\cdot_{y}).

Fix m∈ℤ≥m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}. We claim that, for every j,|α|,|β|≤mj,|\alpha|,|\beta|\leq m,

∂tjM~,∂xαM~,∂yβM~∈L2​(ℝ×ℝn×ℝn).\partial_{t}^{j}\widetilde{M},\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\widetilde{M},\partial_{y}^{\beta}\widetilde{M}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}). (5.9)

Indeed, the assumptions on the xx-derivatives in (5.7) imply that

M∈Hm​(ℝ≥,xn,L2​(ℝt×ℝ≥,yn)).M\in H^{m}\left(\mathbb{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq,x}^{n};L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq,y}^{n})\right).

The boundedness of ℰx\mathscr{E}_{x} described in (5.8) therefore gives

∂xαℰx​M∈L2​(ℝt×ℝxn×ℝ≥,yn),|α|≤m.\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\mathscr{E}_{x}M\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{x}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq,y}),\quad|\alpha|\leq m.

The operator ℰy\mathscr{E}_{y} acts only in the yny_{n}-variable, is bounded on L2L^{2}, and commutes with the xx-derivatives, and so

∂xαM~=∂xαℰy​ℰx​M=ℰy​∂xαℰx​M∈L2​(ℝt×ℝxn×ℝyn),|α|≤m.\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\widetilde{M}=\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\mathscr{E}_{y}\mathscr{E}_{x}M=\mathscr{E}_{y}\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\mathscr{E}_{x}M\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{x}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{y}),\quad|\alpha|\leq m.

Similarly, ℰx\mathscr{E}_{x} commutes with the yy-derivatives and is bounded on L2L^{2}. Hence the assumptions on the yy-derivatives in (5.7) imply

∂yβℰx​M=ℰx​∂yβM∈L2​(ℝt×ℝxn×ℝ≥,yn),|β|≤m.\partial_{y}^{\beta}\mathscr{E}_{x}M=\mathscr{E}_{x}\partial_{y}^{\beta}M\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{x}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq,y}),\quad|\beta|\leq m.

Therefore,

ℰx​M∈Hm​(ℝ≥,yn,L2​(ℝt×ℝxn)).\mathscr{E}_{x}M\in H^{m}(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq,y};L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{x})).

Applying ℰy\mathscr{E}_{y} and using the boundedness described in (5.8) shows

∂yβM~=∂yβℰy​ℰx​M∈L2​(ℝt×ℝxn×ℝyn),|β|≤m.\partial_{y}^{\beta}\widetilde{M}=\partial_{y}^{\beta}\mathscr{E}_{y}\mathscr{E}_{x}M\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{x}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{y}),\quad|\beta|\leq m.

Finally, both extension operators commute with differentiation in tt and are bounded on L2L^{2}, so using the tt-regularity in (5.7), we have

∂tjM~=∂tjℰy​ℰx​M=ℰy​ℰx​∂tjM∈L2​(ℝt×ℝxn×ℝyn),0≤j≤m.\partial_{t}^{j}\widetilde{M}=\partial_{t}^{j}\mathscr{E}_{y}\mathscr{E}_{x}M=\mathscr{E}_{y}\mathscr{E}_{x}\partial_{t}^{j}M\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{x}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{y}),\quad 0\leq j\leq m.

This completes the proof of (5.9).

Letting t∗t^{*}, x∗x^{*}, and y∗y^{*} denote the dual variables to tt, xx, and yy, respectively, taking the Fourier transform of (5.9) shows

∫(|t∗|2​m+|x∗|2​m+|y∗|2​m)​|M~^​(t∗,x∗,y∗)|2​d​t∗​d​x∗​d​y∗<∞.\int\left(\left\lvert t^{*}\right\rvert^{2m}+\left\lvert x^{*}\right\rvert^{2m}+\left\lvert y^{*}\right\rvert^{2m}\right)\left\lvert\widehat{\widetilde{M}}(t^{*},x^{*},y^{*})\right\rvert^{2}\>dt^{*}\>dx^{*}\>dy^{*}<\infty. (5.10)

Because mm was arbitrary, (5.10) implies that M~∈Hm​(ℝ×ℝn×ℝn)\widetilde{M}\in H^{m}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}) for every m∈ℤ≥m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}. The Sobolev embedding theorem then implies that M~​(t,x,y)∈C∞​(ℝ×ℝn×ℝn)\widetilde{M}(t,x,y)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}). Since M=M~|ℝ×ℝ≥n×ℝ≥nM=\widetilde{M}\big|_{\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}}, the result follows. ∎

Proposition 5.6.

Let T⁡(t)T(t) be the strongly continuous semigroup from Lemma 3.1. Then, ∃!Kt(ξ,η)∈C∞((0,∞)×U×U;𝕄M×M(ℂ))\exists\,!K_{t}(\xi,\eta)\in C^{\infty}\left((0,\infty)\times U\times U;\mathbb{M}^{M\times M}(\mathbb{C})\right) such that Kt​(ξ,⋅)∈L2​(U,Vol,𝕄M×M​(ℂ))K_{t}(\xi,\cdot)\in L^{2}\left(U,\mathrm{Vol};\mathbb{M}^{M\times M}(\mathbb{C})\right), ∀(t,ξ)∈(0,∞)×U\forall(t,\xi)\in(0,\infty)\times U, and such that

On U×UU\times U, the kernel of T​(t)∗T(t)^{*} is Kt​(η,ξ)∗K_{t}(\eta,\xi)^{*}, the matrix adjoint of KtK_{t} with the roles of ξ\xi and η\eta reversed. Thus, if 𝒫t,ξ\mathscr{P}_{t,\xi} is any partial differential operator with smooth coefficients in the t,ξt,\xi variables, and ψ∈Ccpt∞​((0,∞)×U×U)\psi\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}\left((0,\infty)\times U\times U\right), then (5.4) applied to both T⁡(t)T(t) and T​(t)∗T(t)^{*} implies

‖𝒫t,ξ​(ψ⁡(t,ξ,η)​Kt​(ξ,η))‖L2​((0,∞)×𝔑×𝔑)+‖𝒫t,η​(ψ⁡(t,ξ,η)​Kt​(ξ,η))‖L2​((0,∞)×𝔑×𝔑)<∞.\left\|\mathscr{P}_{t,\xi}\left(\psi(t,\xi,\eta)K_{t}(\xi,\eta)\right)\right\|_{L^{2}((0,\infty)\times\mathfrak{N}\times\mathfrak{N})}+\left\|\mathscr{P}_{t,\eta}\left(\psi(t,\xi,\eta)K_{t}(\xi,\eta)\right)\right\|_{L^{2}((0,\infty)\times\mathfrak{N}\times\mathfrak{N})}<\infty. (5.11)

Let V1,V2⊆UV_{1},V_{2}\subseteq U be small open neighborhoods of ξ0\xi_{0} and η0\eta_{0}, respectively, which are diffeomorphic to connected open subsets of ℝ≥n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq}. Let ψ∈Ccpt∞​((0,∞)×V1×V2)\psi\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}\left((0,\infty)\times V_{1}\times V_{2}\right) equal 11 on a neighborhood of (t0,ξ0,η0)(t_{0},\xi_{0},\eta_{0}). Equation (5.11) shows that Lemma 5.5 applies, yielding ψ⁡(t,ξ,η)​Kt​(ξ,η)∈C∞​(ℝ×𝔑×𝔑,𝕄M×M​(ℂ))\psi(t,\xi,\eta)K_{t}(\xi,\eta)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathfrak{N}\times\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{M}^{M\times M}(\mathbb{C})). As (t0,ξ0,η0)∈(0,∞)×U×U(t_{0},\xi_{0},\eta_{0})\in(0,\infty)\times U\times U was arbitrary, it follows that Kt​(ξ,η)∈C∞​((0,∞)×U×U,𝕄M×M​(ℂ))K_{t}(\xi,\eta)\in C^{\infty}\left((0,\infty)\times U\times U;\mathbb{M}^{M\times M}(\mathbb{C})\right), as desired. ∎

5.2 Completion of the proof of Theorem 3.14

Proposition 5.6 shows the existence of a smooth kernel K⁡(t,ξ,η)∈C∞​((0,∞)×U×U,𝕄M×M​(ℂ))K(t,\xi,\eta)\in C^{\infty}\left((0,\infty)\times U\times U;\mathbb{M}^{M\times M}(\mathbb{C})\right) satisfying (3.9). It remains to establish (3.10). We establish (3.10) by using the estimates of [Str26] to establish the assumptions of [Str25c, Theorem ], which yields (3.10).1010 10 In [Str25c], the kernel Kt​(ξ,η)K_{t}(\xi,\eta) was scalar valued instead of matrix-valued. However, the same proof applies in the matrix-valued setting. See [Str25c, Remark ]. We apply the results of [Str26, Str25c] without change. The reader will need these two papers at hand to completely follow the proof.

By replacing ℒ\mathscr{L} with ℒ−γ\mathscr{L}-\gamma (i.e., replacing T⁡(t)T(t) with eγ​t​T​(t)e^{\gamma t}T(t) and 𝒬⁡(f,g)\mathcal{Q}(f,g) with 𝒬⁡(f,g)−γ​⟨f,g⟩L2\mathcal{Q}(f,g)-\gamma\langle f,g\rangle_{L^{2}}), it suffices to prove (3.10) in the case γ=0\gamma=0. Note that all the hypotheses of Theorem 3.14 still hold after this replacement (the new estimates depend on γ\gamma, though that does not change the statement of Theorem 3.14).

We turn to proving (3.10) with γ=0\gamma=0. We begin by stating a slightly different result, which implies (3.10). In it, we use the vector fields V0,V1,…,VrV_{0},V_{1},\ldots,V_{r} described in Section 3.

Let δ1=δ1​(𝒦1)>0\delta_{1}=\delta_{1}(\mathcal{K}_{1})>0 be as in Theorem 2.4 (as applied in Section 3).

Proposition 5.7.

∀𝒦⋐U\forall\mathcal{K}\Subset U compact, ∃δ𝒦∈(0,δ1]\exists\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\in(0,\delta_{1}], c𝒦>0c_{\mathcal{K}}>0, for all ordered multi-indices α,β\alpha,\beta, ∀j∈ℤ≥\forall j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}, ∃Cα,β,j,𝒦≥0\exists C_{\alpha,\beta,j,\mathcal{K}}\geq 0, ∀ξ,η∈𝒦\forall\xi,\eta\in\mathcal{K}, ∀t>0\forall t>0,

|∂tjVξα​Vηβ​Kt​(ξ,η)|≤Cα,β,j,𝒦​((ρV​(ξ,η)+t1/2​κ)∧δ𝒦)−2​κ​j−|α|−|β|×exp⁡(−c𝒦​((ρV​(ξ,η)∧δ𝒦)2​κt)12​κ−1)×Vol(BV(ξ,(ρV(ξ,η)+t1/2​κ)∧δ𝒦))−1/2×Vol(BV(η,(ρV(ξ,η)+t1/2​κ)∧δ𝒦))−1/2.\begin{split}\left|\partial_{t}^{j}V_{\xi}^{\alpha}V_{\eta}^{\beta}K_{t}(\xi,\eta)\right|\leq&C_{\alpha,\beta,j,\mathcal{K}}\left(\left(\rho_{V}(\xi,\eta)+t^{1/2\kappa}\right)\wedge\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\right)^{-2\kappa j-|\alpha|-|\beta|}\\ &\times\exp\left(-c_{\mathcal{K}}\left(\frac{\left(\rho_{V}(\xi,\eta)\wedge\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\right)^{2\kappa}}{t}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\kappa-1}}\right)\\ &\times\mathrm{Vol}\left(B_{V}\left(\xi,\left(\rho_{V}(\xi,\eta)+t^{1/2\kappa}\right)\wedge\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\right)\right)^{-1/2}\\ &\times\mathrm{Vol}\left(B_{V}\left(\eta,\left(\rho_{V}(\xi,\eta)+t^{1/2\kappa}\right)\wedge\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\right)\right)^{-1/2}.\end{split} (5.12)

Before we prove Proposition 5.7, we see how it implies (3.10).

Proof of (3.10) given Proposition 5.7.

Because the C∞​(𝔑1,ℝ)C^{\infty}(\mathfrak{N}_{1};\mathbb{R})-module generated by V0,…,VrV_{0},\ldots,V_{r} is the same as the C∞​(𝔑1,ℝ)C^{\infty}(\mathfrak{N}_{1};\mathbb{R})-module generated by W1,…,WrW_{1},\ldots,W_{r}, and since 𝒦⋐U⋐𝔑1\mathcal{K}\Subset U\Subset\mathfrak{N}_{1}, for every L1,L2∈ℤ≥L_{1},L_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq} we have

∑|α|≤L1|β|≤L2|∂tjVξα​Vηβ​Kt​(ξ,η)|≈∑|α|≤L1|β|≤L2|∂tjWξα​Wηβ​Kt​(ξ,η)|,∀ξ,η∈𝒦.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\alpha|\leq L_{1}\\ |\beta|\leq L_{2}\end{subarray}}\left|\partial_{t}^{j}V_{\xi}^{\alpha}V_{\eta}^{\beta}K_{t}(\xi,\eta)\right|\approx\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\alpha|\leq L_{1}\\ |\beta|\leq L_{2}\end{subarray}}\left|\partial_{t}^{j}W_{\xi}^{\alpha}W_{\eta}^{\beta}K_{t}(\xi,\eta)\right|,\quad\forall\xi,\eta\in\mathcal{K}.

Moreover, the right-hand sides of (3.10) and (5.12) are increasing in |α||\alpha| and |β||\beta| (since δ𝒦≤1\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\leq 1).

Vol​(BV​(ξ,(ρV​(ξ,η)+t1/2​κ)∧δ𝒦))1/2​Vol​(BV​(η,(ρV​(ξ,η)+t1/2​κ)∧δ𝒦))1/2≈Vol(BW(ξ,(ρW(ξ,η)+t1/2​κ)∧δ𝒦)),∀t>0,ξ,η∈𝒦.\begin{split}&\mathrm{Vol}\left(B_{V}\left(\xi,\left(\rho_{V}(\xi,\eta)+t^{1/2\kappa}\right)\wedge\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\right)\right)^{1/2}\mathrm{Vol}\left(B_{V}\left(\eta,\left(\rho_{V}(\xi,\eta)+t^{1/2\kappa}\right)\wedge\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\right)\right)^{1/2}\\ &\approx\mathrm{Vol}\left(B_{W}\left(\xi,\left(\rho_{W}(\xi,\eta)+t^{1/2\kappa}\right)\wedge\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\right)\right),\quad\forall t>0,\>\xi,\eta\in\mathcal{K}.\end{split} (5.14)

The remainder of this section is devoted to the proof of Proposition 5.7. Fix a compact set 𝒦⋐U\mathcal{K}\Subset U for which we want to prove Proposition 5.7, and fix ψ∈Ccpt∞​(U)\psi\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}(U) with 0≤ψ≤10\leq\psi\leq 1 and ψ=1\psi=1 on a neighborhood of 𝒦\mathcal{K}. In our application of [Str25c, Theorem ], we make the following choices. For each α\alpha and β\beta, we apply [Str25c, Theorem ] with p0=2p_{0}=2, 𝔑x=𝔑y=𝒦\mathfrak{N}_{x}=\mathfrak{N}_{y}=\mathcal{K}, μ=Vol\mu=\mathrm{Vol}, ω0=0\omega_{0}=0, X=ψ​VαX=\psi V^{\alpha}, Y=ψ​VβY=\psi V^{\beta}, SX​(δ)=ϵα​δ|α|S_{X}(\delta)=\epsilon_{\alpha}\delta^{|\alpha|}, and SY​(δ)=ϵβ​δ|β|S_{Y}(\delta)=\epsilon_{\beta}\delta^{|\beta|}, where ϵα,ϵβ>0\epsilon_{\alpha},\epsilon_{\beta}>0 are small numbers to be chosen later, and we take δ0∈(0,1]\delta_{0}\in(0,1] in that theorem to be another small number to be chosen later. In [Str25c, Theorem ] the constant c>0c>0 is an “admissible constant” (see [Str25c, Definition ]). We will show that such admissible constants do not depend on α\alpha, β\beta, which is how we show c𝒦c_{\mathcal{K}} in Proposition 5.7 does not depend on α\alpha or β\beta; see [Str25c, Remark ] for a further discussion of this point.

Our first issue is that [Str25c] used a globally defined metric, whereas ρV\rho_{V} is only defined on 𝔑1\mathfrak{N}_{1}. Also, we need to choose δ𝒦\delta_{\mathcal{K}}, which is called δ0\delta_{0} in [Str25c]. We continue to use the notation δ0\delta_{0} and choose δ𝒦≔δ0\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\coloneqq\delta_{0} at the end of the proof. The next lemma both exhibits an appropriate global metric and chooses δ0\delta_{0}.

In light of Lemma 5.8, the statement of Proposition 5.7 is unchanged if ρV\rho_{V} and BV​(⋅,⋅)B_{V}(\cdot,\cdot) are replaced throughout by ρ\rho and Bρ​(⋅,⋅)B_{\rho}(\cdot,\cdot). Moreover, in the proof which follows, we only consider BV​(ξ,δ)B_{V}(\xi,\delta) for ξ∈𝒦0\xi\in\mathcal{K}_{0} and δ∈(0,δ0]\delta\in(0,\delta_{0}] and we only consider ρV​(ξ,η)\rho_{V}(\xi,\eta) for ξ,η∈𝒦\xi,\eta\in\mathcal{K}. Thus, we may verify the assumptions of [Str25c] using ρV\rho_{V} even though it is not a globally defined metric, because it agrees with the globally defined metric ρ\rho from Lemma 5.8 wherever we use it. Moreover, by Lemma 5.81, the topology generated by ρ\rho agrees with the usual topology on 𝔑\mathfrak{N}, so we do not need to make the distinction about which topology we are using in the sequel.

We turn to verifying the assumptions of [Str25c, Theorem ] with the above choices.

Lemma 5.9.

For every α\alpha, ψ​Vα:Dom⁡(ℒ∞)→L2​(𝔑,Vol)\psi V^{\alpha}:\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{\infty}\right)\rightarrow L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol}) and ψ​Vα:Dom⁡((ℒ∗)∞)→L2​(𝔑,Vol)\psi V^{\alpha}:\mathrm{Dom}\left(\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right)^{\infty}\right)\rightarrow L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol}) are continuous. By Lemma 5.3, f↦f|Uf\mapsto f\big|_{U} is continuous Dom⁡(ℒ∞)→C∞​(U,ℂM)\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{\infty}\right)\rightarrow C^{\infty}\left(U;\mathbb{C}^{M}\right) and Dom⁡((ℒ∗)∞)→C∞​(U,ℂM)\mathrm{Dom}\left(\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right)^{\infty}\right)\rightarrow C^{\infty}\left(U;\mathbb{C}^{M}\right). Since ψ∈Ccpt∞​(U)\psi\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}(U), g↦ψ​Vα​gg\mapsto\psi V^{\alpha}g is continuous C∞​(U,ℂM)→Ccpt∞​(U,ℂM)↪L2​(𝔑,Vol,ℂM)C^{\infty}\left(U;\mathbb{C}^{M}\right)\rightarrow C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}(U;\mathbb{C}^{M})\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol};\mathbb{C}^{M}). The result follows by composing these two maps. ∎

Lemma 5.10.

𝒟0​(𝔑,ℂM)⊆Dom⁡(ℒ∞)∩Dom⁡((ℒ∗)∞)\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{C}^{M})\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{\infty}\right)\cap\mathrm{Dom}\left(\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right)^{\infty}\right). Moreover, let O⊆𝔑O\subseteq\mathfrak{N} be an open set, and suppose f∈𝒟0​(𝔑,ℂM)f\in\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{C}^{M}) satisfies f|O=0f\big|_{O}=0. Then ℒj​f|O=0=(ℒ∗)j​f|O\mathscr{L}^{j}f\big|_{O}=0=\left(\mathscr{L}^{*}\right)^{j}f\big|_{O}, ∀j∈ℤ≥\forall j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}.

Let ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} be the partial differential operator with smooth coefficients from Assumption 3.6. We prove the following claim by induction on jj. For each j∈ℤ>j\in\mathbb{Z}_{>}, 𝒟0​(𝔑,ℂM)⊆Dom⁡(ℒj)\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{C}^{M})\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{j}\right) and ℒj​f=ℒ0j​f\mathscr{L}^{j}f=\mathscr{L}_{0}^{j}f, ∀f∈𝒟0​(𝔑,ℂM)\forall f\in\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{C}^{M}).

The base case, j=1j=1, is Assumption 3.6. Suppose we have the claim for jj, and let f∈𝒟0​(𝔑,ℂM)f\in\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{C}^{M}). Then, by the base case, f∈Dom⁡(ℒ)f\in\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L}) with ℒ​f=ℒ0​f\mathscr{L}f=\mathscr{L}_{0}f, and so ℒ​f=ℒ0​f∈𝒟0​(𝔑,ℂM)⊆Dom⁡(ℒj)\mathscr{L}f=\mathscr{L}_{0}f\in\mathscr{D}_{0}(\mathfrak{N};\mathbb{C}^{M})\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{j}\right), and so f∈Dom⁡(ℒj+1)f\in\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{j+1}\right). Moreover, we have ℒj+1​f=ℒ​ℒj​f=ℒ​ℒ0j​f=ℒ0j+1​f\mathscr{L}^{j+1}f=\mathscr{L}\mathscr{L}^{j}f=\mathscr{L}\mathscr{L}_{0}^{j}f=\mathscr{L}_{0}^{j+1}f, where the second equality used the inductive step, while the third used the base case. This completes the induction and the proof for ℒ\mathscr{L}. Since our assumptions are symmetric in ℒ\mathscr{L} and ℒ∗\mathscr{L}^{*} (see Remark 3.16), the result for ℒ∗\mathscr{L}^{*} follows as well.

(Vξ,δ,2)γ​a~α,β∘Ψξ,δ=((δ​V)γ​a~α,β)∘Ψξ,δ,\left(V^{\xi,\delta,2}\right)^{\gamma}\tilde{a}_{\alpha,\beta}\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}=\left(\left(\delta V\right)^{\gamma}\tilde{a}_{\alpha,\beta}\right)\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta},

To prove Proposition 5.162,4 for (ξ,δ)∈𝒮1(\xi,\delta)\in\mathcal{S}_{1} we will apply [Str26, Corollary ] with ℒ\mathscr{L}, WW, σ\sigma, aα,βa_{\alpha,\beta}, and NN replaced with ℒξ,δ,1\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,1}, Vξ,δ,1V^{\xi,\delta,1}, hξ,δ,1h_{\xi,\delta,1}, aα,βξ,δ,1a_{\alpha,\beta}^{\xi,\delta,1}, and 11, respectively. To prove Proposition 5.162,4 for (ξ,δ)∈𝒮2(\xi,\delta)\in\mathcal{S}_{2} we will apply [Str26, Corollary ] with ℒ\mathscr{L}, WW, σ\sigma, and aα,βa_{\alpha,\beta} replaced with ℒξ,δ,2\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,2}, Vξ,δ,2V^{\xi,\delta,2}, hξ,δ,2h_{\xi,\delta,2}, and aα,βξ,δ,2a_{\alpha,\beta}^{\xi,\delta,2}, respectively. Importantly, all the hypotheses of [Str26, Corollaries and ] hold uniformly in (ξ,δ)(\xi,\delta), and therefore the conclusions also hold uniformly in (ξ,δ)(\xi,\delta) (as is explicitly stated in those results). We turn to filling in the details. We use the notation Q>n​(δ):={(x′,xn)∈Qn​(δ):xn>0}Q^{n}_{>}(\delta):=\left\{(x^{\prime},x_{n})\in Q^{n}(\delta):x_{n}>0\right\}.

The relevance of ℒξ,δ,k\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,k}, k=1,2k=1,2, comes from the next lemma.

Lemma 5.20.

For f∈Dom⁡(ℒ)f\in\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L}),

ℒξ,δ,1​(f∘Φξ,δ)=(δ2​κ​ℒ​f)∘Φξ,δ,(ξ,δ)∈𝒮1,\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,1}\left(f\circ\Phi_{\xi,\delta}\right)=\left(\delta^{2\kappa}\mathscr{L}f\right)\circ\Phi_{\xi,\delta},\quad(\xi,\delta)\in\mathcal{S}_{1}, (5.30)
ℒξ,δ,2​(f∘Ψξ,δ)=(δ2​κ​ℒ​f)∘Ψξ,δ,(ξ,δ)∈𝒮2,\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,2}\left(f\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}\right)=\left(\delta^{2\kappa}\mathscr{L}f\right)\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta},\quad(\xi,\delta)\in\mathcal{S}_{2}, (5.31)

where (5.30) is interpreted in the sense of distributions and (5.31) is interpreted in the sense of 𝒟0′\mathscr{D}_{0}^{\prime}.

Proof.

We prove (5.31); the proof of (5.30) is nearly identical. Let f∈Dom⁡(ℒ)f\in\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L}) and G∈𝒟0​(Q≥n​(1),ℂM)G\in\mathscr{D}_{0}(Q^{n}_{\geq}(1);\mathbb{C}^{M}). By Assumption 3.6, we have G∘Ψξ,δ−1∈Dom⁡(ℒ)⊆Dom⁡(𝒬)G\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}^{-1}\in\mathrm{Dom}(\mathscr{L})\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}(\mathcal{Q}). Also, using Theorem 2.410, we have supp⁡(G∘Ψξ,δ−1)⊆Ω\supp(G\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}^{-1})\subseteq\Omega. Therefore, using (5.24) and Assumption 3.5, we have

Vol⁡(BV​(ξ,δ))​⟨G,hξ,δ,2​(δ2​κ​ℒ​f)∘Ψξ,δ⟩L2​(ℝ≥n)=δ2​κ​⟨G∘Ψξ,δ−1,ℒ​f⟩L2​(𝔑,Vol)=δ2​κ​𝒬​(G∘Ψξ,δ−1,f)=δ2​κ​𝒬F​(G∘Ψξ,δ−1,f)=Vol⁡(BV​(ξ,δ))​𝒬ξ,δ,2​(G,f∘Ψξ,δ)=Vol⁡(BV​(ξ,δ))​⟨G,hξ,δ,2​ℒξ,δ,2​(f∘Ψξ,δ)⟩L2​(ℝ≥n),\begin{split}&\mathrm{Vol}(B_{V}(\xi,\delta))\left\langle G,h_{\xi,\delta,2}\left(\delta^{2\kappa}\mathscr{L}f\right)\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}\right\rangle_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq})}=\delta^{2\kappa}\left\langle G\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}^{-1},\mathscr{L}f\right\rangle_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}\\ &=\delta^{2\kappa}\mathcal{Q}\left(G\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}^{-1},f\right)=\delta^{2\kappa}\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{F}}\left(G\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}^{-1},f\right)=\mathrm{Vol}(B_{V}(\xi,\delta))\mathcal{Q}^{\xi,\delta,2}(G,f\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta})\\ &=\mathrm{Vol}(B_{V}(\xi,\delta))\left\langle G,h_{\xi,\delta,2}\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,2}\left(f\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}\right)\right\rangle_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq})},\end{split} (5.32)

where the last equality used the definitions of 𝒬ξ,δ,2\mathcal{Q}^{\xi,\delta,2} and ℒξ,δ,2\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,2} (see (5.22) and (5.29)). Dividing both sides of (5.32) by Vol​(BV​(ξ,δ))\mathrm{Vol}(B_{V}(\xi,\delta)) gives

⟨G,hξ,δ,2​(δ2​κ​ℒ​f)∘Ψξ,δ⟩L2​(ℝ≥n)=⟨G,hξ,δ,2​ℒξ,δ,2​(f∘Ψξ,δ)⟩L2​(ℝ≥n),∀G∈𝒟0​(Q≥n​(1),ℂM),\left\langle G,h_{\xi,\delta,2}\left(\delta^{2\kappa}\mathscr{L}f\right)\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}\right\rangle_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq})}=\left\langle G,h_{\xi,\delta,2}\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,2}\left(f\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}\right)\right\rangle_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq})},\quad\forall G\in\mathscr{D}_{0}(Q^{n}_{\geq}(1);\mathbb{C}^{M}),

completing the proof. ∎

Lemma 5.21.

∀G∈L2​(Qn​(1),ℂM)\forall G\in L^{2}\left(Q^{n}(1);\mathbb{C}^{M}\right), ∀(ξ,δ)∈𝒮1\forall(\xi,\delta)\in\mathcal{S}_{1},

Lemma 5.22.

[Str26, Assumptions and ] hold. Namely, ∃D1,D2≥0\exists D_{1},D_{2}\geq 0 such that the following statements hold.

  1. 1.

    ∀(ξ,δ)∈𝒮1∩(𝒦0×(0,δ0])\forall(\xi,\delta)\in\mathcal{S}_{1}\cap\left(\mathcal{K}_{0}\times(0,\delta_{0}]\right), ∀G∈Ccpt∞​(Qn​(1/2),ℂM)\forall G\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}\left(Q^{n}(1/2);\mathbb{C}^{M}\right),

(5.35)
  2. 2.

    ∑|α|=κ‖(Vξ,δ,2)α​G‖L2​(ℝ≥n)2≤D1​Re⁡𝒬ξ,δ,2​(G,G)+D2​‖G‖L2​(ℝ≥n)2.\sum_{|\alpha|=\kappa}\left\|\left(V^{\xi,\delta,2}\right)^{\alpha}G\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq})}^{2}\leq D_{1}\Real\mathcal{Q}^{\xi,\delta,2}(G,G)+D_{2}\left\|G\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq})}^{2}. (5.36)
Proof.

Using (5.21) and (5.29), we see

⟨G,hξ,δ,1​ℒξ,δ,1​G⟩L2​(ℝn)=𝒬ξ,δ,1​(G,G),∀G∈Ccpt∞​(Qn​(1/2),ℂM).\left\langle G,h_{\xi,\delta,1}\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,1}G\right\rangle_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}=\mathcal{Q}^{\xi,\delta,1}(G,G),\quad\forall G\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}\left(Q^{n}(1/2);\mathbb{C}^{M}\right).

∑|α|=κ‖(Vξ,δ,1)α​G‖L2​(ℝn)2≤D1​Re⁡𝒬ξ,δ,1​(G,G)+D2​‖G‖L2​(ℝn)2.\sum_{|\alpha|=\kappa}\left\|\left(V^{\xi,\delta,1}\right)^{\alpha}G\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}^{2}\leq D_{1}\Real\mathcal{Q}^{\xi,\delta,1}(G,G)+D_{2}\left\|G\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}^{2}.

After making this replacement, the proofs of 1 and 2 are nearly identical, so we prove only 2.

∑|α|≤κ‖Vα​f‖L2​(𝔑,Vol)2≈∑|α|≤κ‖Wα​f‖L2​(𝔑,Vol)2≲|𝒬⁡(f,f)|+‖f‖L2​(𝔑,Vol)2.\sum_{|\alpha|\leq\kappa}\left\|V^{\alpha}f\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}^{2}\approx\sum_{|\alpha|\leq\kappa}\left\|W^{\alpha}f\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}^{2}\lesssim\left|\mathcal{Q}(f,f)\right|+\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}^{2}. (5.37)

∑|α|≤κ‖Vα​f‖L2​(𝔑,Vol)2≤C1​Re⁡𝒬F​(f,f)+C2​‖f‖L2​(𝔑,Vol)2,∀f∈𝒟0​(U,ℂM).\sum_{|\alpha|\leq\kappa}\left\|V^{\alpha}f\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}^{2}\leq C_{1}\Real\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{F}}(f,f)+C_{2}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}^{2},\quad\forall f\in\mathscr{D}_{0}(U;\mathbb{C}^{M}). (5.39)

Multiplying both sides of (5.39) by δ2​κ\delta^{2\kappa}, for δ∈(0,δ0]\delta\in(0,\delta_{0}] (and restricting the sum to |α|=κ|\alpha|=\kappa) gives

∑|α|=κ‖(δ​V)α​f‖L2​(𝔑,Vol)2≤C1​Re⁡δ2​κ​𝒬F​(f,f)+C2​δ2​κ​‖f‖L2​(𝔑,Vol)2≤C1Reδ2​κ𝒬F(f,f)+C2∥f∥L2​(𝔑,Vol)2,∀f∈𝒟0(U;ℂM).\begin{split}&\sum_{|\alpha|=\kappa}\left\|\left(\delta V\right)^{\alpha}f\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}^{2}\leq C_{1}\Real\delta^{2\kappa}\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{F}}(f,f)+C_{2}\delta^{2\kappa}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}^{2}\\ &\leq C_{1}\Real\delta^{2\kappa}\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{F}}(f,f)+C_{2}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}^{2},\quad\forall f\in\mathscr{D}_{0}(U;\mathbb{C}^{M}).\end{split} (5.40)

Thus, f∈Ccpt∞​(U∩Int⁡(𝔑),ℂM)⊆𝒟0​(U,ℂM)f\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}(U\cap\Int(\mathfrak{N});\mathbb{C}^{M})\subseteq\mathscr{D}_{0}(U;\mathbb{C}^{M}). Applying (5.40) with this choice of ff, and freely using Lemma 5.21, we see

Vol⁡(BV​(ξ,δ))​∑|α|=κ‖(Vξ,δ,2)α​G‖L2​(ℝ≥n)2≈Vol⁡(BV​(ξ,δ))​∑|α|=κ‖(Vξ,δ,2)α​G​(y)‖L2​(ℝ≥n,hξ,δ,2​(y)​d​y)2=∑|α|=κVol⁡(BV​(ξ,δ))​‖((δ​V)α​f)∘Ψξ,δ​(y)‖L2​(ℝ≥n,hξ,δ,2​(y)​d​y)2=∑|α|=κ‖(δ​V)α​f‖L2​(𝔑,Vol)2≤C1​Re⁡δ2​κ​𝒬F​(f,f)+C2​‖f‖L2​(𝔑,Vol)2=C1​Re⁡Vol⁡(BV​(ξ,δ))​𝒬ξ,δ,2​(G,G)+C2​‖f‖L2​(𝔑,Vol)2,\begin{split}&\mathrm{Vol}(B_{V}(\xi,\delta))\sum_{|\alpha|=\kappa}\left\|\left(V^{\xi,\delta,2}\right)^{\alpha}G\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq})}^{2}\approx\mathrm{Vol}(B_{V}(\xi,\delta))\sum_{|\alpha|=\kappa}\left\|\left(V^{\xi,\delta,2}\right)^{\alpha}G(y)\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq};h_{\xi,\delta,2}(y)dy)}^{2}\\ &=\sum_{|\alpha|=\kappa}\mathrm{Vol}(B_{V}(\xi,\delta))\left\|\left(\left(\delta V\right)^{\alpha}f\right)\circ\Psi_{\xi,\delta}(y)\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq};h_{\xi,\delta,2}(y)dy)}^{2}=\sum_{|\alpha|=\kappa}\left\|\left(\delta V\right)^{\alpha}f\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}^{2}\\ &\leq C_{1}\Real\delta^{2\kappa}\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{F}}(f,f)+C_{2}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}^{2}=C_{1}\Real\mathrm{Vol}(B_{V}(\xi,\delta))\mathcal{Q}^{\xi,\delta,2}(G,G)+C_{2}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathfrak{N},\mathrm{Vol})}^{2},\end{split} (5.41)

Lemma 5.23.

For (ξ,δ)∈𝒮2∩(𝒦0×(0,δ0])(\xi,\delta)\in\mathcal{S}_{2}\cap\left(\mathcal{K}_{0}\times(0,\delta_{0}]\right), 𝒟ξ,δ⊆Ccpt∞((−15/32,15/32);C∞(Q≥n(1);ℂM))\mathcal{D}_{\xi,\delta}\subseteq C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{cpt}}\left((-15/32,15/32);C^{\infty}\left(Q^{n}_{\geq}(1);\mathbb{C}^{M}\right)\right).

Proof.

Thus far, we have verified the assumptions of [Str26, Corollaries and ]. Those corollaries give uniform subelliptic estimates for ∂t+ℒξ,δ,1\partial_{t}+\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,1} and ∂t+ℒξ,δ,2\partial_{t}+\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,2}. We use this to obtain the next result, where we only consider functions in the null space of either ∂t+ℒξ,δ,1\partial_{t}+\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,1} or ∂t+ℒξ,δ,2\partial_{t}+\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,2}. For it we use the non-isotropic Sobolev spaces Hs​(ℝ1+n)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{1+n}) and Hs​(ℝ≥1+n)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{1+n}_{\geq}) defined in (5.1) and (5.2).

    ‖ϕ1​U‖Hl+1​(ℝ≥1+n)≤Cl​‖ϕ2​U‖L2​(ℝ≥1+n).\|\phi_{1}U\|_{H^{l+1}(\mathbb{R}^{1+n}_{\geq})}\leq C_{l}\|\phi_{2}U\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{1+n}_{\geq})}.

The key to this result is that we have verified the assumptions of [Str26, Sections and ] uniformly in (ξ,δ)(\xi,\delta), and so the results in those sections give estimates which are uniform in (ξ,δ)(\xi,\delta); indeed, those results state explicitly what their estimates depend on.

In both cases, 1 and 2, Theorem 2.414 shows the vector fields V0ξ,δ,k,…,Vrξ,δ,kV_{0}^{\xi,\delta,k},\ldots,V_{r}^{\xi,\delta,k}, k=1,2k=1,2, are Hörmander vector fields uniformly in (ξ,δ)(\xi,\delta). Moreover, Theorem 2.412,13 show that for (ξ,δ)∈𝒮2(\xi,\delta)\in\mathcal{S}_{2}, V0ξ,δ,2,…,Vrξ,δ,2V_{0}^{\xi,\delta,2},\ldots,V_{r}^{\xi,\delta,2} are of the same form as the vector fields studied in [Str26, Section ]. For 2, we apply [Str26, Corollary ] (with 𝒟1=𝒟ξ,δ\mathcal{D}_{1}=\mathcal{D}_{\xi,\delta}) to see that for U∈𝒟ξ,δU\in\mathcal{D}_{\xi,\delta},

‖ϕ1U‖Hl+1​(ℝ≥1+n)≤Cl(‖ϕ2(∂t+ℒξ,δ,2)U‖Hl+1−ϵ0​(ℝ≥1+n)+‖ϕ2U‖L2​(ℝ≥1+n)),\begin{split}&\left\|\phi_{1}U\right\|_{H^{l+1}(\mathbb{R}^{1+n}_{\geq})}\leq C_{l}\left(\left\|\phi_{2}\left(\partial_{t}+\mathscr{L}^{\xi,\delta,2}\right)U\right\|_{H^{l+1-\epsilon_{0}}(\mathbb{R}^{1+n}_{\geq})}+\left\|\phi_{2}U\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{1+n}_{\geq})}\right),\end{split} (5.60)

for some ϵ0>0\epsilon_{0}>0. Since U∈𝒟ξ,δU\in\mathcal{D}_{\xi,\delta}, (5.43) shows U⁡(t,x)=θ⁡(t)​u​(t,Ψξ,δ​(x))U(t,x)=\theta(t)u(t,\Psi_{\xi,\delta}(x)), where u:(−1/2,1/2)→Dom(ℒ∞)u:(-1/2,1/2)\rightarrow\mathrm{Dom}\left(\mathscr{L}^{\infty}\right) is a (−ℒ,ξ,δ)(-\mathscr{L},\xi,\delta)-heat function. |(Vξ,δ,1)α​U​(t,y)|≲∑|β|≤|α||∂yβU⁡(t,y)|,\left|\left(V^{\xi,\delta,1}\right)^{\alpha}U(t,y)\right|\lesssim\sum_{|\beta|\leq|\alpha|}\left|\partial_{y}^{\beta}U(t,y)\right|, (5.65)

Theorem 2.411(k.ii) shows
